{"id": "268fe20c-cb76-4027-a0d9-9f83c673c026", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "thinking", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "The data-01 volume stands out as gp2 at 100GB, giving it a baseline of only 300 IOPS with burst capacity to 3000 - this makes it a strong candidate for burst balance exhaustion issues.

System status checks all look healthy with no failures, so I need to dig into CloudWatch metrics next. With seven data volumes to review, I'll prioritize BurstBalance on data-01 while also pulling VolumeQueueLength, VolumeTotalWriteTime, and VolumeWriteOps across all volumes to pinpoint the actual bottleneck.

I also want instance-level CPUUtilization and NetworkOut, though disk metrics like DiskWriteBytes may not exist by default under AWS/EC2 unless the CloudWatch agent is running. Comparing the incident window (23:13:46 to 23:28:46) against the prior hour as baseline, I'll structure a get_metric_data call with multiple queries covering each volume's write ops, write time, and queue length.

I'm second-guessing whether EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% apply here, since those burst-balance metrics are really meant for burstable EBS-optimized instance types like t3, not m5.xlarge, so I'll stick to the simpler CPUUtilization, NetworkOut, and EBSWriteOps metrics at the instance level.

I'm planning to pull all these metrics via a single get_metric_data call with multiple queries rather than many separate get_metric_statistics calls, using a 60-second period for the incident window and a 5-minute period for the hour-long baseline window to keep data volume manageable while still capturing Average, Maximum, and Sum statistics.

I'm cataloguing the EBS volumes attached to this instance along with their types and throughput/size configurations to make sure I query the right volume IDs for root and data disks.

Since the task is about slow disk writes generally and I don't know which volume the app writes to, I'll need to check VolumeQueueLength and compute write latency (VolumeTotalWriteTime/VolumeWriteOps) across all volumes, plus BurstBalance for the gp2 volume specifically.

That amounts to roughly 33 EBS queries plus 5 instance-level metrics (CPUUtilization, NetworkOut, EBSWriteOps, EBSWriteBytes, StatusCheckFailed), totaling around 38 queries, which should fit within a single get_metric_data call's limit. I'll run this for the incident window first, then repeat for the baseline window.

Since get_metric_data only accepts one time range per call, I need two separate calls. Given the complexity of building the full query list for every volume and metric, it might be smarter to first narrow down which volume is actually showing anomalies before querying everything exhaustively.

The write ops jumped sharply around 23:21, going from near-zero to tens of thousands per minute.

This looks like a ramp-up pattern where write demand suddenly spiked and saturated the volume's IOPS ceiling about 5-6 minutes ago, staying pinned there since. I want to pull baseline data from the prior hour for write ops, total write time, and queue length to confirm whether this saturation is unusual or a recurring pattern, and I should also check CPU utilization since it's sitting near 1%, which rules out compute as the cause.

With CPU clearly not a factor and network output only modest at 20-30KB/s, disk looks like the real bottleneck on data-02 hitting its 3000 IOPS ceiling. I also want to dig into CloudTrail for any recent volume modifications, resizes, or instance type changes, and compare baseline metrics for data-02 against the other volumes -- it's notable that data-03 through data-07 show zero activity, and even data-01's gp2 volume has no writes and full burst balance.

The root volume shows minimal activity too, so data-02 is clearly the one doing real work, matching up with /dev/sdg as the main application data mount. I'll pull its baseline metrics from the prior hour and check CloudTrail for volume modify events.
